## Redraft

This is a redraft of `preamble.qmd` under the `writing-scientific-books` skill,
kept beside the original for comparison. Content is unchanged in substance. What
changed is who the prose addresses, how many claims arrive with an instance
attached, and how much of it there is.

# The reader

This book is written for one person, and it is worth saying who before saying
anything else.

She is intelligent, she reads widely, and she is not a spatial analyst. She may
be a forester who has spent fifteen years in stands and has never opened a
geographic information system. She may be a carbon project developer who
commissions the maps and signs the report. She may be a verifier who has to
decide whether a number is defensible, having been trained in forestry rather
than in geodesy. She may be a graduate student who can fit a mixed model and has
never been told what a projection does to a hectare.

What she has in common across all four is the thing this book is built on. She is
perfectly capable of the material and nobody has taught it to her in order,
because the people who write about it already know it and have forgotten that
they had to learn it. Every chapter is written on the assumption that she will
follow any argument put in front of her and will not follow a term that arrives
undefined.

So no term appears here before the sentence that introduces it. When you meet
*support*, meaning the patch of ground one number describes, it will be
explained in the sentence you meet it in, and it will be explained with a picture
rather than with three more words you also do not know.

# The book

This book teaches the measurement of forest carbon from satellite and airborne
observation, and it teaches it from the beginning. That second half is a
deliberate choice and it is what separates this book from what sits beside it on
the shelf.

The remote sensing literature is superb and it starts in the middle. Open almost
any recent volume on forest observation and the first chapter maps canopy height
from radar, or fuses two satellite records to model the mass of wood standing in
a stand, or corrects the position of laser footprints fired from orbit. Every one
of those chapters is excellent. Every one of them assumes you already know what a
coordinate system does to an area calculation, why a stack of satellite images is
a solid rather than a pile of pictures, and where the uncertainty in a reported
tonne actually comes from.

The two literatures fail to meet, and they fail in opposite directions. The
methods literature will teach you to reproject a raster and never mention what a
verifier does with the result. The standards documents start on the far side of
the same gap and will tell you that an uncertainty deduction is required without
ever showing you how to compute one. In practice the two get reconciled in an
undocumented spreadsheet on one analyst's laptop, and that is where forest
monitoring systems fail. They fail from workflows nobody else can run and
documentation nobody wrote, far more often than they fail from flawed science.

So the book walks a trajectory rather than presenting a collection. The early
chapters put a shapefile and a raster in your hands, establish what a projection
does to a hectare, and settle what a number refers to before any number is
reported. Those chapters are not remedial. The errors that cost a project its
credits are almost always made in the first hour of the work, in a transformation
nobody wrote down or a mask applied in the wrong order, and by the time they
surface in an audit they are buried under six months of analysis that looks
impeccable. Chapter 1 makes the point with a single forest plot whose claimed
area and mapped area differ by 6.6 per cent, with no survey error anywhere in it.
Building the foundation slowly is the cheapest uncertainty reduction available.

Each chapter then adds one layer and closes on a number a verifier would accept,
so that a reader who began by reading a shapefile finishes by pushing allometric
error through a simulation and converting the result into the credits a project
gives up for being imprecise.

# The code

Everything here runs. The book is written in Quarto, every figure and every
number in the text is produced by code that ships with it, and the whole thing
builds offline on a laptop with no account, no cloud credit and no network.

That is not a convenience. A verifier has to be able to re-run your work three
years later on a different machine, and an analysis that cannot be re-run has not
been documented, only described. Where a registry document is cited the citation
gives the section and the equation, so you can check it against the original
rather than take my word for it.

# The pleasure

What I hope carries through all of it is the reason any of us do this work. There
is a particular pleasure in looking at a planet you have only ever stood on and
slowly acquiring the tools to map it, to measure it, and to say something about
it that holds up. I have tried to write a book that keeps hold of that rather
than assuming the reader arrived already fluent.

# The spine

Recorded 4 September 2026 and amended 5 September 2026. This is the thread that
opens in chapter 1, is picked up in every chapter, and closes in the final part.
It exists so that no chapter can be written without knowing what it owes the arc.

## The thread

**The geometry you compute on, and the support your answer has.**

Both halves are needed and they are not the same question. Geometry is where the
arithmetic happens, on a plane, on a sphere, on an ellipsoid, in a projected grid
that stretches area as you move away from the equator. Support is what the answer
refers to, the area or the interval or the volume over which a value was measured
and to which it applies.

An example of each, because neither survives on its own. A polygon drawn round a
forest plot has an area of 27.30 hectares if you wrap it in an upright box and
25.56 if you follow the trees, and that is geometry. A reflectance value from a
satellite describes a 20 metre square of ground, so a value sitting on a forest
edge describes half a canopy and half a clearing and belongs to neither, and that
is support. Every number in forest carbon accounting has both. Almost no report
states either. The errors that survive to an audit are nearly always one of them.

It is the only question genuinely present in every chapter, from reading a
shapefile to reporting a deduction, and it is the question the field's own
literature treats as settled and has not.

## The close

Amended 5 September 2026. The closing message of the book is disturbance ecology,
and the data cube is the instrument that makes it arguable rather than the
destination. By the final part the reader has a cube fit for spatial modelling,
and the question the book asks of it is whether a forest carbon landscape has
states, whether it can pass between them, and whether a monitoring system built
from these observations could tell.

That takes the argument into tipping behaviour, into regime shift in ecosystem
change and forest carbon flux, and into Markov chain Monte Carlo as the machinery
for inference about a system that changes over time and is observed with error.

It does not displace the design-based against model-based distinction after
Pebesma. It contains it, because asking whether a system has changed regime is a
question about what the data can support, and the honest answer needs the
inferential frame the earlier chapters built. The sentence a reader should be able
to say at the end is that they know the geometry, the support, the inferential
frame, and what all three together permit them to claim about whether the forest
is the same forest.

## The return

The last chapter goes back to the first. The reader is shown the same polygon from
chapter 1 and asked what its area is now. The honest answer is that it depends on
the geometry, the engine, the support and the inferential frame, all four of which
they can now state. That is the arc, and it is the difference between a book that
teaches operations and one that teaches judgement.

\newpage

# House rule

Every chapter enters through something concrete and physical, reaches a
methodological question by the middle, closes on a number a verifier would
accept, and states somewhere what geometry the arithmetic happened on and what
support the answer has.

Each one carries a single methodological question, an entry that earns its place,
and an edge that does not flinch. The board at
<https://claude.ai/code/artifact/4499bb90-ae13-4fdd-8051-ee6e63d01c74> holds all
seventeen with their questions, their entries, their edges and their sources.

# One paragraph

From `publishing/book-proposal.md`, kept here because it is the same argument in
the register a publisher reads.

Carbon projects are audited on numbers that come out of a geographic information
system, and almost nobody who audits them was trained to build one. This book
teaches the spatial analysis that forest carbon verification actually rests on,
from reading a shapefile to reporting an uncertainty deduction, and it does so
with the primary registry documents open beside the code.

# Open decisions

Four, all recorded on the chapter board and none of them settled.

1. Does one of the last chapters carry the dynamical-systems close explicitly?
   The seventeen-chapter outline as briefed spreads it across chapters 12, 13 and
   the closing part, so no chapter owns it and none is accountable for it.
2. Does the subtitle going to Elsevier name disturbance ecology? It currently
   promises lidar, radar and optical data in mensuration, monitoring and
   inventory, and none of those three is the closing argument.
3. Is the page budget 400 pages or 560? *Satellite Remote Sensing for Forest and
   Environmental Monitoring* runs 20 chapters over 663 pages, so 33 a chapter puts
   seventeen at about 560 before front matter.
4. Does the baseline chapter lose the word *counterfactual*? It appears nine times
   in that chapter's prose and the standing style rule excludes terms imported
   from programme evaluation where the field's own wording exists.

# Where it lives

Four files carry the argument. `publishing/preamble-draft.md` holds the preamble
and the author biography. `publishing/book-spine.md` holds the thread, with its
5 September amendment. `index.qmd` is the preface as it stands in the book.
`publishing/book-proposal.md` holds the same argument in the register a publisher
reads. None is rendered by the book project, because all four are planning files
rather than chapters.
